concepts.title: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence' refers to.
questions.a: At the time of independence in 1947, the Indian economy was characterised by low level of economic development, stagnant agriculture, underdeveloped industry, high dependence on the primary sector, widespread poverty, and an exploitative colonial economic structure geared towards serving British interests rather than Indian development.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence'.
questions.a: The colonial economy was marked by agricultural stagnation, deindustrialisation, poverty and a lopsided structure designed to benefit Britain, leaving India with low income and weak infrastructure at independence.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Indian Economy 1947-90

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Agriculture Sector during 1947-90' refers to.
questions.a: After independence, agriculture was the backbone of the Indian economy but suffered from low productivity, dependence on monsoon and exploitative land relations. Reforms included abolition of zamindari, land ceiling laws, consolidation of holdings and the introduction of institutional and technological changes to raise productivity.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Agriculture Sector during 1947-90'.
questions.a: Land reforms and technological change (Green Revolution) were the two pillars of agricultural development strategy during 1947-90.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Agriculture Sector during 1947-90' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Indian Economy 1947-90

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Industry Sector during 1947-90' refers to.
questions.a: The industrial sector during 1947-90 was developed through Five Year Plans with emphasis on public sector investment in heavy and basic industries, import substitution and protection. The state controlled key industries through licensing, leading to industrial growth but also inefficiency and a protected domestic market.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Industry Sector during 1947-90'.
questions.a: Industrialisation was state-led, import-substituting and public-sector dominated, with the licensing system (permit raj) controlling private investment.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Industry Sector during 1947-90' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Indian Economy 1947-90

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Five Year Plans' refers to.
questions.a: The Five Year Plans were the framework of centralised economic planning in India starting from 1951, aimed at achieving growth, modernisation, self-reliance and equity. The First Plan focused on agriculture, the Second on heavy industry, and subsequent plans addressed diverse goals of the economy over successive five-year cycles.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Five Year Plans'.
questions.a: Planning through Five Year Plans emphasised public investment, industrialisation, self-reliance and social justice as key objectives.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Five Year Plans' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Indian Economy 1947-90

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'New Economic Policy 1991' refers to.
questions.a: The New Economic Policy of 1991 was a package of structural reforms introduced to overcome the balance of payments crisis and fiscal deficit of the late 1980s. It was based on the LPG framework - Liberalisation, Privatisation and Globalisation - aimed at reducing the role of the state and increasing the role of the market in the economy.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'New Economic Policy 1991'.
questions.a: The 1991 reforms marked a shift from a planned, protected economy to a market-oriented, open economy through the LPG approach.

questions.q: Under which section is 'New Economic Policy 1991' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Economic Reforms since 1991

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Liberalisation' refers to.
questions.a: Liberalisation refers to the removal or reduction of government controls, regulations and restrictions on economic activities. In India, it included dismantling industrial licensing, reforming the financial sector, tax reforms, and reducing tariffs and quantitative restrictions on foreign trade to allow greater freedom to private enterprise.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Liberalisation'.
questions.a: Liberalisation freed the private sector from licensing and controls, reformed finance and taxation, and opened trade to increase efficiency and competition.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Liberalisation' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Economic Reforms since 1991

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Privatisation' refers to.
questions.a: Privatisation refers to the transfer of ownership, management or control of public sector enterprises to the private sector. It aims to improve efficiency, reduce the government's financial burden and foster competition. In India, it took the form of disinvestment of public sector undertakings and dereservation of industries reserved for the public sector.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Privatisation'.
questions.a: Privatisation reduces government involvement in business through disinvestment and dereservation, aiming to improve efficiency and reduce fiscal burden.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Privatisation' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Economic Reforms since 1991

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Globalisation' refers to.
questions.a: Globalisation is the process of integration of a country's economy with the world economy through reduction of trade barriers, free movement of goods, services, capital and technology, and greater openness to foreign investment. In India, it involved reducing tariffs, removing quantitative restrictions on imports and encouraging foreign direct investment.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Globalisation'.
questions.a: Globalisation integrates the domestic economy with the world economy through trade liberalisation, foreign investment and technology flows.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Globalisation' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Economic Reforms since 1991

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'LPG Reforms and Their Impact' refers to.
questions.a: The LPG reforms (Liberalisation, Privatisation and Globalisation) introduced since 1991 transformed the Indian economy from a controlled, protected system to a market-oriented, open economy. Their impact includes higher growth, a larger services sector, greater foreign investment and trade, but also rising inequality, displacement of small producers and concerns about agriculture and employment.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'LPG Reforms and Their Impact'.
questions.a: LPG reforms boosted growth, services and external integration, but also created challenges of inequality, agrarian distress and jobless growth.

questions.q: Under which section is 'LPG Reforms and Their Impact' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Economic Reforms since 1991
